name: Giant's Grave
text: Your train passes near Giant's Grave, on the train's {side}, a pair of standing stones at the foot of Black Combe. The smaller stone is carved with three cup and ring marks, the taller with just one.

name: St George's Church, Millom
text: Your train passes near St George's Church, Millom, on the train's {side}, built between 1874 and 1877 to a design by the Lancaster architects Paley and Austin. Of its cost of about £12,000, Millom Ironworks gave £7,186, and its spire is a landmark in the town.

name: Foxfield
text: Your train passes Foxfield, on the train's {side}, a village on the Duddon Estuary just outside the Lake District National Park. Its station was once where a branch line to Broughton-in-Furness and Coniston began.

name: Kirkby-in-Furness
text: Your train passes near Kirkby-in-Furness, on the train's {side}, a village made up of six hamlets looking out over the Duddon Estuary. Much of it grew up around the Burlington Slate Quarries, once linked to the railway by a rope-worked narrow-gauge line known as the Long Incline.

name: Duddon Inshore Rescue
text: Your train passes near the base of Duddon Inshore Rescue, on the train's {side}, a volunteer search and rescue service set up in 1969 to help people in difficulty in the tidal Duddon Estuary. Its first boat, a small inflatable, went into service in June 1970.

name: Holker Street
text: Your train passes near Holker Street, on the train's {side}, home of Barrow AFC since 1909. The Furness Railway had used the site as a rubbish tip, and refuse in the pitch was a nuisance for years; 16,874 people crammed in for an FA Cup tie against Swansea Town in 1954.

name: Barrow Park
text: Your train passes near Barrow Park, on the train's {side}, 45 acres designed by Thomas Mawson in 1908 and laid out over the following two decades. It was built on what was then the edge of town and is now more or less central, with a boating lake and a miniature railway.

name: Furness Abbey
text: Your train passes Furness Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 1123 by Stephen, Count of Boulogne, and built of local sandstone in the 'Vale of Nightshade'. Before the Dissolution it was the second-wealthiest Cistercian monastery in England, after Fountains Abbey.

name: Dalton Castle
text: Your train passes near Dalton Castle, on the train's {side}, a 14th-century peel tower built when the Scots were raiding Furness. It was Furness Abbey's courthouse and prison, stayed a courthouse for more than three centuries after the Dissolution, and has belonged to the National Trust since 1965.

name: Lindal railway incident
text: Your train passes the spot near Lindal-in-Furness where, on September 22nd 1892, the ground opened up beneath Furness Railway engine No. 115 as it shunted in the sidings. The driver jumped clear and the engine fell into the hole; it was never recovered and still lies buried beneath the railway.

name: Leven Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the River Leven on Leven Viaduct, opened in 1857 with a section at its western end that could slide back to let ships through. That was fixed in place in 1866, and after a train was blown over on the viaduct in a storm in 1903, a wind gauge was put in so that it could be closed in high winds.

name: Flookburgh
text: Your train passes near Flookburgh, on the train's {side}, an old village where cockle and shrimp fishing play a big part in life. Stan Laurel, born in Ulverston in 1890, often came here by train as a boy to visit his uncle and aunt, who ran the village's co-operative store.

name: Grange Lido
text: Your train passes Grange Lido, on the train's {side}, an Art Deco open-air pool 50 metres long, opened on the promenade in 1932 and filled with sea water at high tide. It closed in 1993, and the shifting course of the River Kent now leaves the sea some way off, beyond the salt marsh.

name: Arnside Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the River Kent on Arnside Viaduct, about 505 metres long on 51 piers, where the river runs out into Morecambe Bay. Built between 1856 and 1857, it was the first viaduct in the world to have its piles dug by water jetting.

name: Trowbarrow Quarry
text: Your train passes near Trowbarrow Quarry, on the train's {side}, a limestone quarry that started work when this railway opened in 1857 and closed in 1959. A new way of making tarmacadam was developed here, mixing crushed limestone with hot tar from Carnforth's gasworks; it is now a nature reserve and a popular place for rock climbing.

name: RSPB Leighton Moss
text: Your train passes RSPB Leighton Moss, on the train's {side}, the largest area of reed bed in north-west England, home to bearded tits, marsh harriers, bitterns, otters and red deer. Richard Gillow drained it for farming with steam power after 1822, but by 1918 it had flooded again.

name: Carnforth MPD
text: Your train passes near Carnforth's old engine shed, on the train's {side}, finished by the London, Midland and Scottish Railway in 1944, late in the age of steam. It later became the Steamtown Carnforth museum, and is now the main operating base of West Coast Railways.

name: Midland Hotel, Morecambe
text: Your train passes near the Midland Hotel, on the train's {side}, built in 1933 by the London, Midland and Scottish Railway to a Streamline Moderne design by Oliver Hill, with sculpture by Eric Gill. Its murals by Eric Ravilious were later destroyed, but the hotel itself has been restored.

name: Heysham nuclear power station
text: Your train passes near Heysham's nuclear power stations, on the train's {side}: two separate stations side by side, each with two advanced gas-cooled reactors. In 2016 a reactor at the newer station, Heysham 2, broke the world record for running continuously without being shut down.

name: Lancaster Castle
text: Your train passes near Lancaster Castle, on the train's {side}, most likely founded between 1092 and 1094 on the site of a Roman fort above a crossing of the River Lune. It was first used as a prison in 1196 and was one until 2011, and it belongs to the sovereign as Duke of Lancaster.

name: Greenhalgh Castle
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Greenhalgh Castle, on the train's {side}, built near Garstang in 1490 by Thomas Stanley, 1st Earl of Derby. In the Civil War it was one of the last two Royalist strongholds in Lancashire to give in, surrendering in May 1645 after a bitter siege, and was then partly pulled down.

name: St Walburge's Church, Preston
text: Your train passes near St Walburge's Church, on the train's {side}, a Roman Catholic church designed by Joseph Hansom, who also designed the hansom cab. Its spire is the tallest of any parish church in England.

name: Christ Church, Wesham
text: Your train passes near Christ Church, Wesham, on the train's {side}, designed by the Lancaster architects Paley, Austin and Paley and consecrated in 1894. It was a chapel of ease to Kirkham's parish church until 1913, when it was given a parish of its own.

name: Railway Hotel, Kirkham
text: Your train passes the Railway Hotel, Kirkham, on the train's {side}, built around 1850, about a decade after the Preston and Wyre Railway arrived; metal letters on its roof still spell out "THE RAILWAY". In 1996 a network of tunnels was found behind its cellars.

name: St Chad's Church, Poulton-le-Fylde
text: Your train passes near St Chad's Church, Poulton-le-Fylde, on the train's {side}, on a site with a church by the 11th century and perhaps before the Norman Conquest. Its tower dates from the 17th century, and inside are a Georgian staircase, a Jacobean pulpit and box pews.

name: Layton cemetery
text: Your train passes near Layton cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1873 when Blackpool's parish churchyard had run out of room. It first had three chapels, Anglican, Catholic and Nonconformist; only the Anglican one is left.

name: Wrea Green
text: Your train passes near Wrea Green, on the train's {side}, a village round the largest village green in Lancashire, with a duck pond known locally as "The Dub". Plagued by sparrows in 1897, the parish council paid a halfpenny for every sparrow, sparrow's egg or rat's tail brought in.

name: Lytham Windmill
text: Your train passes near Lytham Windmill, on the train's {side}, a tower mill built on the marshes around 1805. In 1919 a high wind overcame its brake, the sails spun out of control and the mill burnt out; it now belongs to the town and holds a museum of flour milling.

name: Lytham Hall
text: Your train passes near Lytham Hall, on the train's {side}, a Georgian country house built for Thomas Clifton between 1757 and 1764 to a design by John Carr of York. It is the only Grade I listed building in the Borough of Fylde.

name: Royal Lytham & St Annes Golf Club
text: Your train passes Royal Lytham & St Annes Golf Club, on the train's {side}, founded in 1886, which has hosted the Open Championship 11 times and the Ryder Cup twice. George V made it "Royal" shortly before its first Open, in 1926, and its links course has 167 bunkers.

name: St Annes Pier
text: Your train passes near St Annes Pier, on the train's {side}, completed in 1885 as one of the first public buildings in the planned resort of St Annes. Changes to the Ribble's channels for Preston Dock later left it on dry land, ending its steamers to Blackpool and Liverpool.

name: The Big One
text: Your train passes The Big One, on the train's {side}, a roller coaster 65 metres high that opened at the Pleasure Beach on May 28th 1994 as the tallest in the world. It cost £12 million, and its track and supports were airlifted to Blackpool from Bolton.

name: Grand National
text: Your train passes the Grand National, on the train's {side}, a wooden roller coaster built in 1935 by the American engineer Charles Paige, on which two cars race each other. It is one of only two surviving wooden coasters laid out as a Möbius loop, and was listed at Grade II in 2017.

name: Penwortham Old Bridge
text: Your train passes near Penwortham Old Bridge, on the train's {side}, five stone arches over the Ribble opened in 1759, after a first bridge here, finished in 1755, collapsed the next year. Until the early 20th century it was the lowest bridge across the river.

name: Rufford Old Hall
text: Your train passes near Rufford Old Hall, on the train's {side}, built for the Hesketh family late in the 15th century or early in the 16th, and now the National Trust's. Its great hall has the only known surviving 16th-century carved screen of bog oak, and its gardens a giant pair of topiary squirrels.

name: Burscough
text: Your train passes near Burscough, on the train's {side}, a town with Viking roots: its name comes from Burh-skogr, "fortress in the woods". The remains of a large Roman fort, begun in the first century, have been found here, a rare Roman site for the west of Lancashire.

name: Burscough Priory
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Burscough Priory, on the train's {side}, an Augustinian house founded around 1190 by Robert Fitz-Henry and dissolved around 1536. Several members of the Stanley family, the earls of Derby, were buried there.

name: Church of St Peter and St Paul, Ormskirk
text: Your train passes near Ormskirk's Church of St Peter and St Paul, on the train's {side}, which dates from no later than the 12th century. It is one of only three churches in England with both a tower and a spire, and the only one with both at the same end.

name: Argleton
text: Your train passes near where Argleton was supposed to be, on the train's {side}: a place that appeared on Google Maps, though there were only empty fields here. Other web services took it as real, giving its weather and listing local businesses there, until Google removed it.

name: Aughton, Lancashire
text: Your train passes near Aughton, on the train's {side}, a village between Ormskirk and Maghull. In 2025 its three fine-dining restaurants, Moor Hall, The Barn and sō-lō, held five Michelin stars between them.
